title: What is Java Flight Recorder (JFR), and how do you use it for low-overhead production profiling (GC, allocations, thread contention, hotspots)?
shortTitle: Java Flight Recorder (JFR) — low-overhead production profiling

s1_definition.profdef: JFR is a low-overhead (~1-2%) profiling and diagnostics framework built into the JVM (free since Java 11, previously commercial in Oracle JDK). It records JVM events — GC pauses, memory allocations, thread contention, CPU hotspots, I/O latency, class loading — into a binary `.jfr` file that can be analyzed with JDK Mission Control (JMC). Start with: `java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar` or programmatically. Key advantage: always-on production monitoring with minimal performance impact.

When something goes wrong (performance issue), you review the recording (jfr file) to find the cause. Unlike security cameras, JFR costs almost nothing in resources (~1% overhead).

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JFR is a low-overhead (~1-2%) profiling and diagnostics framework built into the JVM (free since Java 11, previously commercial in Oracle JDK). It records JVM events — GC pauses, memory allocations, thread contention, CPU hotspots, I/O latency, class loading — into a binary `.jfr` file that can be analyzed with JDK Mission Control (JMC). Start with: `java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar` or programmatically. Key advantage: always-on production monitoring with minimal performance impact.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** JFR is like the bank's security cameras that record EVERYTHING — transactions, employee movements, system access — with minimal impact on daily operations. When something goes wrong (performance issue), you review the recording (jfr file) to find the cause. Unlike security cameras, JFR costs almost nothing in resources (~1% overhead).

**One line to remember:** JFR = built-in JVM profiler, ~1% overhead, records GC/alloc/threads/CPU, analyze with JMC. -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr.

sections.s2_technical:
Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is a low-overhead profiling and event-recording framework built into the JVM (free since Java 11). It continuously records events — method sampling, allocation, garbage collection, locks, I/O, exceptions — into a compact binary `.jfr` file that you analyse later with JDK Mission Control or the `jfr` tool.

Its key property is low overhead, typically a few percent, so you can run it in PRODUCTION rather than only in a lab. You start it on the command line (`-XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr`) or at runtime with `jcmd <pid> JFR.start`. You can also emit custom application events by extending `jdk.jfr.Event`, which lets a banking service record domain events like "settlement batch completed" with timing and metadata.

A banking example: a settlement service suffering intermittent latency spikes in production enables JFR to capture allocation and lock contention during the incident window, then Mission Control shows the hot path. Senior nuance: JFR complements metrics and traces — metrics tell you SOMETHING is slow, JFR tells you WHY at the JVM/allocation/lock level, with far less overhead than a traditional sampling profiler.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A settlement service showed intermittent latency spikes only in production, where attaching a heavy profiler was unacceptable. Fix: Java Flight Recorder runs with a few percent overhead, capturing allocation, GC, and lock events into a `.jfr` file during the incident so the team can diagnose the root cause offline.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: a settlement for trade TRD-001 that takes 42 ms, recorded as a JFR event.

**Step 2.** `event.begin()` marks the start timestamp inside the JVM recording.

**Step 3.** The domain fields tradeId and millis are set — custom metadata that appears in Mission Control.

**Step 4.** `event.end()` (and commit) writes the event into the low-overhead `.jfr` buffer.

**Step 5.** In production the recording is dumped to a file and analysed offline to find why latency spiked.

```text
INFO: JFR event Settlement Completed tradeId=TRD-001 millis=42
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ JFR USAGE ═══

  Command-line:
    java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar

  Programmatic:
    Recording recording = new Recording();
    recording.start();
    ... application runs ...
    recording.stop();
    recording.dump(Path.of("app.jfr"));

  Analyze:
    Open app.jfr in JDK Mission Control (JMC)
    → GC pauses, memory leaks, thread contention, CPU hotspots

  ═══ WHAT JFR RECORDS ═══

  GC events:      pause times, frequency, memory before/after
  Allocations:    which methods allocate the most objects
  Thread:         contention (locks), deadlocks, park/unpark
  CPU:            hotspot methods, execution samples
  I/O:            file read/write latency, socket activity
  Class loading:  which classes loaded, time spent
  Custom events:  your own @Event classes (TradeExecution, etc.)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java Flight Recorder is a production-safe profiling tool built into the JVM since Java 11 (free). It records JVM events with ~1-2% overhead — safe for always-on monitoring. Start recording with `-XX:StartFlightRecording` command-line flag or programmatically with the `jdk.jfr.Recording` API. Analyze the .jfr file with JDK Mission Control for GC pauses, memory allocation hotspots, thread contention, and CPU profiling. You can also create custom events by extending `jdk.jfr.Event` — useful for recording business-level metrics like trade execution time alongside JVM-level diagnostics.
